proposed_edges.relationship: Cronon criticizes Turner’s vague frontier categories and 1890 closure, replacing homogeneous frontier stages with differentiated regional connections (1987).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected printed 158–167,174–176. The account of previous critics is distinguished from Cronon’s own regional alternative. Criticism is not wholesale rejection: he retains Turner’s interdisciplinary questions;165n 28 expressly distinguishes writing from teaching.

proposed_edges.relationship: Turner remains an explicitly acknowledged organizing foil for Cronon’s teaching and questions about regional environments, despite Cronon’s criticism (1987).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 160n 14 describes Cronon’s own course organization;175–176 recovers continuing questions. An acknowledged critical resource, not endorsement of the frontier thesis or a teacher–student relationship.

proposed_edges.relationship: White reads Turner’s settlement story alongside Buffalo Bill’s conquest story as complementary frontier myths that marginalize Indigenous dispossession (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected White transcription corroborated by Richard W. Steele’s complete 1995 scholarly review. Exact book pagination and illustrations uncollated; the full chapter remains unread. This is White’s interpretation of Turner, not independent validation of every exhibition object.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hofstadter criticizes Turner’s weak critical response to expansion, Indigenous dispossession and anti-Mexican and anti-Chinese nativism, as quoted by Bogue (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bogue 206 and 220n 38 visually checked. His quotation identifies The Progressive Historians,104,106 in a 1969 manifestation. Hofstadter’s original chapter and 1949 essay remain unread; the claim is expressly mediated by Bogue.

proposed_edges.relationship: Deloria criticizes Turner’s frontier boundary for naturalizing Indigenous difference and an expectation of inevitable white triumph (2002).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher excerpt 8–10, with 6–7 framing. Deloria situates Turner within a longer frontier paradigm; this neither makes Turner its sole inventor nor treats all Indigenous historiography as one position. Remaining chapter unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Taylor criticizes the continued use of Turner’s racial and national types in Kluger’s expansion narrative, arguing for differentiated Indigenous and colonial histories (2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own scholarly review paragraphs on Turner and Kluger, especially “Like Turner, Kluger insists” and the French-war comparison. The immediate object is Kluger’s recycled Turner; his attributed Limerick quotation is not assigned to Taylor as original wording. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wolfe explicitly agrees that frontier closure marks a major change, interpreting the post-frontier shift through Indigenous containment and assimilation within continuing settler colonialism (2013).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary 257–259, especially 258, and 276 n 19. Qualified agreement is not blanket defense or proved influence. This remains an undirected comparison/reception link; Native sovereignty and continuing elimination remain central to Wolfe’s different account.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foner explicitly identifies Black Reconstruction and Du Bois’s account of the Civil War as resources for his interpretation of emancipation and revolution.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Foner’s own 2015 answers recount using Black Reconstruction and expressly identify his agreement with Du Bois. This is a bounded acknowledgment, not proof of every influence on Foner or a claim that his family acquaintance alone establishes intellectual transmission.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly acknowledges Bourdieu’s sociology as an influence on the collective development of socio-history while declining school allegiance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer. The collective is described by Noiriel as including his own generation and practice; no formal master–disciple relation or adoption of all Bourdieu’s positions is asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Bourdieu’s later public interventions for presenting political judgments with the undifferentiated authority of researched scholarship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Second 2012 answer on fundamental research and essays, explicitly naming Raisons d’Agir interventions. This is Noiriel’s critique of the distinction between expertise and public intervention, not a rejection of all Bourdieu’s sociology.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly uses Wittgenstein’s game and language-game metaphor to explain socio-history as shared rules of practice rather than an all-purpose theory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer, paragraph beginning “La socio-histoire, ce n’est pas une théorie.” A named methodological metaphor, not blanket adoption of Wittgenstein’s philosophy.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tilly contests Vernon’s linguistic explanation and subjectivist definition of democracy, arguing that Vernon’s own evidence also supports a modest expansion of democratic control (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected journal review 260–262 and 265–268 opening. Tilly also praises Vernon’s empirical richness and raises competing criteria, not an independently settled verdict. Mixed edge_1161 remains because it includes other readers and later works.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tilly criticizes Joyce’s treatment of class and language for obscuring relational agency and causal explanation, while valuing the empirical research (1994).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected review 260–265. Tilly’s account is attributed; the underlying book is not independently adjudicated here. The mixed debate summary and its other named critics remain intact.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and the sharp opposition between individual resistance and collective revolt, while affirming the book’s lasting value (2001).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete scholarly rereading. Johnson argues for coerced rule and a continuum of resistance; he explicitly rejects the simplistic charge that Genovese denied enslaved people agency. Original historical examples and Roll, Jordan, Roll remain uncollated.

proposed_edges.relationship: Genovese adapts Gramscian hegemony to explain how paternalist relations could mediate slaveholding class rule, as Walter Johnson explicates (2001).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Johnson’s own substantive account distinguishes Genovese’s use of hegemony from denying agency and then criticizes its application. Named-reader mediation is explicit; no certification of Genovese’s full book or Gramsci originals. The existing mixed Genovese/Gutman edge_162 stays.

proposed_edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly credits Cohen’s Chicago research while placing greater weight on Prohibition and the election of 1928 in the formation of cross-ethnic political loyalties (2016).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: McGirr’s own answer to the Making a New Deal question. She calls the emphases distinct but not incompatible; this is an acknowledged debt and extension, not a claim that she repudiates Cohen or derives all her work from her.

proposed_edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly agrees with Gerstle’s account of the American state as unevenly powerful, connecting public/private authority and federal tensions to Prohibition (2016).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own answer on the weak-state myth names both Gerstle and Novak. This link records her specific agreement with Gerstle’s formulation; Novak is not merged into him. Agreement alone does not prove transmission, so the link stays undirected.

previous_record.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
previous_record.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
